data.title: High Expectations Of Delayed Home Ownership
data.description:
For the past two years, the housing narrative has been dominated by a single number: the thirty-year mortgage rate. With rates remaining high relative to pandemic-era lows, consensus expectations imply homebuilding is a cyclical business in retreat, waiting for the Federal Reserve to rescue it. In many ways, this view is understandable. A buyer who locked in a low rate is reluctant to sell, and a buyer shopping today faces a payment that looks unforgiving next to the one her neighbor enjoys. Put differently, the market has spent its energy debating the price of money and very little asking who is forming households, and what, precisely, they are willing to buy.

For more than a decade following the Great Financial Crisis, the United States built fewer homes than its population growth, household formation, and aging housing stock required. Builders and their lenders had been scarred by the bust, and land developers were wiped out in great numbers. Housing starts recovered slowly and remain below trend growth today. A shortage of this kind does not disappear because the mortgage rate fluctuates in a given quarter; it is cured only by construction, and construction is being constrained by the same high rates that frighten investors.

The demand side is where we have variant perceptions. While the affordability problem is real: rates, taxes, insurance, and down payments have made ownership expensive for many lower- and middle-income households, we observe the narrower cohort of married, college-educated, dual-income couples without children, who have adequate credit and income yet remain renters for partially non-economic reasons. Many of them will pay as much each month for a small city-center apartment as a suburban mortgage would cost at 6-7% rates and still decline the house. The decision is not rent versus buy. It is a walkable, flexible, experience-rich life versus a suburban or exurban home surrounded by identical structures, a Target (TGT) Supercenter, a Home Depot (HD), and perhaps even a Buc-ee’s. Put in those terms, the rent is not the obstacle; the trade is.

Large builders solve affordability with cheap land and a standardized product. This manufacturing assembly line produces a product that is spacious, with spare bedrooms, a yard, and a two-car garage space. What the buyer surrenders is time, since a longer commute works as an implicit mortgage attached to the cheaper house, walkability, and identity, since the standardized subdivision offers little of it. For a childless couple, the extra bedrooms and the school district are excess capacity, a payment today for a contingent future use. The apartment’s rewards are immediate and visible; the house’s are deferred and conditional. Adding children on top of this is another expense that conflicts directly with their budget for (yet another) trip to Tuscany.

There is also a psychological element, one that we believe social media has amplified. Prior generations measured their standard of living against relatives, coworkers, and the neighbors visible from the front porch. Today’s young adults measure theirs against an algorithm that overweights the exceptional: the best restaurant, the renovated kitchen, the vacation, the promotion. They compare those highlights with their own complete budget, commute, and ordinary weekdays, while the hidden inputs of parental help and “sponsorship” go unseen. Researchers such as Juliet Schor, Ethan Kross, and Philippe Verduyn have documented how reference groups and passive scrolling breed upward comparison and envy. Vacations are photogenic and rewarded with attention; the joys of home ownership as defined by property taxes, insurance, and HVAC replacements are not. Keeping up appearances means immediate gratification, while the long-run gains of ownership appear nearly invisible.

This creates a coordination problem the market under-appreciates, because houses and children are complements. A couple says it will buy when it is ready for children, and that it will have children once it is settled in the right house, and the apartment-and-delay equilibrium can persist for years. We believe shifting lifestyle choices therefore postpone household formation rather than abolish it altogether. The $64,000 question is if many of these couples will eventually buy when children arrive, when travel and “big dumb lines” lose their marginal appeal.

NVR (NVR), D.R. Horton (DHI), and Lennar (LEN) share a characteristic that is easy to overlook in a debate about rates: each has changed the way it does business. NVR has long favored lot options over owning large amounts of land, keeping its capital employed low and its returns high. D.R. Horton has paired its scale and inventory discipline with a growing rental and lot-development business that diversifies its earnings. Lennar has also moved towards a land-light model, and is making the boldest bet on a housing start recovery by keeping volumes constant at the expense of near-term profitability. Each path differs slightly, but we believe each leads to a business that earns more per dollar invested and is far less vulnerable to the land write-downs that devastated the industry in the 2008 financial crisis.

The balance sheets tell the same story. The homebuilders of the last cycle entered the downturn burdened with debt and overpriced land, and many did not survive it. Today, the three companies we own carry modest leverage, hold substantial liquidity, and continue to repurchase shares at what we believe are attractive prices. In many ways, a company that can use a period of high rates to buy back stock, take share from weaker competitors, and secure land on favorable terms is being strengthened by the very conditions that are causing the industry to be shunned by investors today.

Housing starts may or may not return to trend, the birth rate may or may not recover, and mortgage rates may or may not decline. Regardless of these outcomes, we believe the through-cycle margins, the return on capital, and the balance sheet strength of NVR (NVR), D.R. Horton (DHI), and Lennar (LEN) are improving. In a market fixated on the price of money, we prefer to own the companies that are laser-focused on per-share value creation regardless of the state of the yield curve or the latest viral trend.

data.title: Bitcoin Bearish Signals Deepen As Demand Contracts By 400K BTC
data.description:
Bitcoin's (BTC) bearish outlook has intensified as weakening demand, rising realized losses and deteriorating market sentiment point to further pressure on the top crypto.

Bitcoin demand contracts at fastest pace since July

In a Wednesday report, on-chain analytics firm CryptoQuant stated that Bitcoin's demand growth has contracted at its fastest pace since July 1, with declining spot demand leading the downturn.

According to the report, total Bitcoin demand growth has fallen below -400,000 BTC on a 30-day basis. Spot demand returned to negative territory in early September, while perpetual futures demand also turned negative in early November as traders sold and liquidated leveraged long positions.

Bitcoin: Spot and Perpetual Futures Demand Growth (30-day sum, # of Bitcoin). Source: CryptoQuant

​CryptoQuant said a sustainable recovery would require demand growth to stop contracting, particularly through renewed spot buying rather than increased speculative activity in derivatives markets.

“The first constructive sign would be the 30-day total moving back toward zero, led by spot buying rather than by new leverage in the perpetual futures markets,” the report stated.

Bitcoin holders realize largest daily losses since July

The declining market has also pushed investors to sell their Bitcoin holdings below acquisition prices.

CryptoQuant reported that holders realized net losses of 25,800 BTC during the recent sell-off, marking the largest daily reading since July 13. The development reverses the trend from late August through October, when Bitcoin holders consistently realized profits as prices climbed toward $80,000.

“Loss realization on this scale was last seen in June and July, when Bitcoin was trading in the low $60Ks,” CryptoQuant wrote.

Bitcoin: Daily Net Realized Profit and Loss (# of Bitcoin). Source: CryptoQuant

The report noted that the latest reading indicates that investors who accumulated Bitcoin during the rally are now selling below their cost basis, a pattern associated with bearish market conditions.

Traders return to unrealized losses amid market dip

Another indicator of the market's deterioration is the decline in traders' unrealized profit and loss margin to -20%, its lowest level since July 1. CryptoQuant stated that the reading indicates active traders are holding substantial unrealized losses, placing Bitcoin back in what it describes as a value zone.

“It peaked at 33% in late September, when the price was trading well above traders' cost basis, crossed below zero in early November and has now dropped to -20%,” the report stated.

Historically, similar levels of unrealized losses have coincided with “price bottoming formations.” However, the report cautioned that these formations typically take at least two months before a sustainable recovery begins.

Bitcoin: Onchain Trader Realized Price and Profit/Loss Margin.* Source: CryptoQuant

​Meanwhile, the report highlights a significant concentration of long-term holder spending between $62,000 and $65,000. The range represents an area where new investors accumulated Bitcoin from long-term holders, potentially establishing a support zone around their acquisition prices.

The report warned that a sustained breakdown below $62,000 could weaken this potential support by pushing recent buyers into unrealized losses.

CryptoQuant also highlighted deteriorating analyst sentiment. Only 58% of analysts remain bullish on Bitcoin, down from 77% on October 7.

Additionally, the Bull Score Index has dropped to 10, placing Bitcoin firmly in the extreme bear phase. The index briefly fell to zero on November 10, when Bitcoin was still trading around $74,000.

CryptoQuant said the reading “indicates there are no conditions for a sustainable price recovery and rally.”

Bitcoin is trading at $62,380, down nearly 2% in the past 24 hours at the time of writing.

data.title: Clearing The Decks Ahead Of Anthropic’s Record IPO
data.description:
• Anthropic’s record offering is drawing enormous demand, but the scramble for allocations may be taking a toll on existing portfolios.

• Nvidia (NVDA)’s spectacular post-earnings reversal leaves an awkward question hanging over the AI trade, even as the broader equity tape tells a more complicated story.

• The Fed is still sharpening its claws, although crude oil has unexpectedly come to the Treasury market’s rescue.

• Gold, Bitcoin (BTC.X) and copper are getting caught in the crossfire, with liquidity and positioning increasingly dictating the price action.

Clearing the Decks

Wall Street spent another session clearing the decks ahead of Anthropic’s (ANT) record IPO, and the selling is beginning to resemble the scramble for cash we saw around SpaceX’s June debut. At least that’s what desk chatter this morning suggests.

Nvidia gave back every penny of its post-earnings rally and finished down roughly 3%, while the S&P 500 stumbled and bumbled through a fifth straight decline, repeatedly failing to reclaim its 200-day moving average. Gold, copper and Bitcoin were hammered, but Treasuries rallied for a third day, and King Dollar climbed to fresh 18-month highs in what can best be described as safe-haven demand. A messy tape, but one that makes considerably more sense when you consider how much capital is being shuffled around ahead of Thursday’s opening bell.

Anthropic reportedly priced at $83 a share, above the marketed $70–$78 range, with the offering increased to raise at least $68 billion. Add the $26 billion private placement, and you’re looking at more than $94 billion, comfortably eclipsing SpaceX’s $86.2 billion including its overallotment. The book is reportedly six times oversubscribed. Plenty of demand, certainly, but that money has to come from somewhere, and the market isn’t exactly swimming in spare liquidity.

The Anthropic Shuffle

The five-session comparison with SpaceX is revealing. Ahead of that flotation, retail investors sold existing technology winners to raise cash, with Micron (MU), Qualcomm (QCOM), Broadcom (AVGO), AMD (AMD) and Super Micro (SMCI) among the casualties.

Vanda Research recorded three consecutive sessions of net selling in individual stocks, something not seen since the early pandemic.

The pattern ahead of Anthropic looks familiar, with software shares taking particular punishment and tokenized Anthropic exposure tracking Nvidia lower in recent weeks. That doesn’t mean every sale is funding an IPO allocation, but I’d be surprised if a transaction approaching $100 billion wasn’t forcing some fairly uncomfortable portfolio decisions.

Nvidia’s performance was especially ugly. The stock rallied more than 5% during Colette Kress’s earnings call, only to finish roughly 3% lower despite another outstanding quarter. Reports that Arm’s Rene Haas has been approached about the CEO position have kept the leadership question alive, while Nvidia’s market value remains some $2.1 trillion below its October peak.

Still, Wednesday wasn’t quite the wholesale equity liquidation suggested by the headlines. The Nasdaq finished higher, the Magnificent Seven outperformed the other 493 S&P constituents, software recovered some ground, and cybersecurity shares benefited from the recent string of technology disruptions. The Dow took the worst beating, with UnitedHealth (UNH) under pressure.

Under the hood, Goldman Sachs’ desk flows showed trading activity 20% below the recent two-week average. Hedge funds were 6% better buyers, albeit with a 56% short ratio, while long-only accounts were 15% better sellers, particularly across technology, materials and communication services. Credit was similarly mixed, with modest spread widening but little fresh deterioration in hyperscaler or data-centre credit.

The tape looks more like a market rearranging its risk than one abandoning it altogether. The question is whether Anthropic attracts new capital or simply vacuums up money that would otherwise have supported existing positions.

Oil Gives Bonds a Break, but the Fed Isn’t Finished

The October FOMC minutes offered precious little encouragement for anyone expecting the Fed to blink. Nearly all policymakers anticipate further tightening, while Christopher Waller has kept a potential 50-basis-point December move in the conversation. The market still assigns that outcome only a 10–15% probability, with plenty of tightening already reflected in the curve.

Yet Treasuries rallied, helped by a rather brutal session in crude oil.

WTI fell 4% to $81.50 and Brent dropped 2.5% to around $91 after US crude inventories jumped 3.38 million barrels against expectations of roughly one million. Gasoline stocks surged by more than five million barrels, while distillates also exceeded forecasts. Even with total crude inventories still about 3% below the five-year seasonal average, the physical numbers were bearish enough to drown out the latest Gulf headlines.

And those headlines weren’t exactly reassuring. US strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island, continuing tanker attacks around Hormuz and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries would ordinarily have the oil bulls reaching for higher targets. Instead, smaller tankers are helping maintain Gulf shipments, with October flows reportedly reaching a wartime high.

Oil is trading the barrels, not the bombs. Until the physical supply picture deteriorates, traders appear more interested in swelling inventories than another round of military escalation.

The crude selloff took some heat out of inflation expectations, helping the 10-year Treasury yield retreat toward 5.05%, with the long end rallying about five basis points and a solid 20-year auction adding support. The dollar nevertheless strengthened as hawkish Fed expectations and defensive demand kept the greenback firmly bid.

The Liquidity Trade Gets Ugly

Gold plunged nearly 3% below $3,750, silver tested $44, copper continued its rout, and Bitcoin took another beating. Some of that selling may reflect investors raising cash for Anthropic, particularly in crypto, although the broader hawkish Fed environment is doing plenty of damage without any help from the IPO.

Gold’s behaviour is especially instructive. We’ve been distinguishing between liquidity and solvency for weeks. Bullion can be attractive longer-term insurance against financial instability while still being one of the first things sold when investors need cash. Central banks may keep accumulating, but that doesn’t prevent leveraged holders from liquidating positions when losses elsewhere demand attention.

Copper has a different problem. The speculative premium attached to AI infrastructure and US tariff expectations is being stripped out even as physical supply remains tight. That’s increasingly looking like a reassessment of industrial demand as well as a positioning unwind.

Bitcoin, meanwhile, remains particularly vulnerable as fast money shrinks its risk budget. The proximity to Anthropic’s debut raises the possibility of IPO-related cash raising, but the selling also fits the wider retreat from speculative exposure.

For Thursday, the real test isn’t whether Anthropic produces a spectacular opening print. With an order book this heavily subscribed, a lively debut is hardly an outrageous expectation. What matters is whether the buying spreads beyond the new issue.

I’d be watching Nvidia, software breadth, long-only flows and the S&P 500’s repeated failure at its 200-day moving average. If Anthropic rallies while existing tech names remain offered, Wall Street may have simply swapped one crowded trade for another.

The market has spent the week selling yesterday’s favourites to make room for tomorrow’s biggest IPO. Anthropic may arrive to a standing ovation, but I’d be more interested in seeing whether anybody is still buying once the opening applause dies down.

data.title: SLR Investment Corp.: An 11% Yielder In Flux
data.description:
SLR Investment Corp. (Nasdaq: SLRC) calls itself a “yield-oriented business development company”.

The stock lives up to its billing, with a dividend yield of 11%.

Let’s take a look to see whether investors can rely on the double-digit yield in the future.

SLR Investment invests in senior secured loans to private companies.

As of September 30, SLR had 27 loans worth $178 million outstanding, including…

  • $2 million at 10.84%, maturing in 2027, to All States Ag Parts, a supplier of tractor and combine parts in De Soto, Iowa

  • $9.8 million at 9.15% with a 2029 maturity to CVAUSA Management, a cardiovascular physicians group located in eight states

  • $8 million at 8.75% that matures in 2030 to NS and Associates, a provider of construction services in Parkton, Maryland.

To measure a BDC’s ability to pay its dividend, we look at net interest income, or NII. That’s the difference between how much the company earns in interest from its loans, minus its borrowing and other costs.

In 2025, SLR’s NII fell $10 million to $143 million. This year, it is forecast to inch forward to $146 million.

However, this year’s expectation is still below 2023’s $151 million.

This is important because the Safety Net model penalizes companies when one-year and three-year cash flow growth (or NII growth for BDCs) is negative.

To have confidence that a dividend is rock-solid, we want to see near- and intermediate-term cash flow growth. When those numbers are declining instead, that can be an early warning of a dividend cut.

Last year, SLR paid shareholders $90 million in dividends for a payout ratio of 63%. This year, the payout ratio is projected to dip to 61%. Anything below 100% for a BDC is fine.

The company had paid a $0.41 quarterly dividend (or monthly dividends equal to that amount) since 2018 until it reduced the payout to $0.31 earlier this year. It also cut the dividend in 2013, but that is outside of our 10-year lookback. Safety Net doesn’t penalize companies for dividend cuts that occurred more than 10 years ago, but the reduction earlier this year does knock SLR’s grade down a notch.

The final numbers for 2026 could have a significant impact on the dividend safety rating. If the full-year NII result is north of $151 million, the stock will receive an upgrade. If it’s below last year’s total of $143 million, there will be another downgrade.

For now, there is high risk of a dividend cut.

Dividend Safety Rating: D

data.title: Ranked: The World’s 50 Most Valuable Companies, Including Anthropic
data.description:
Anthropic hasn’t sold a single share to the public yet, but its IPO price range already puts it among the world’s most valuable companies.

This graphic ranks the world’s 50 most valuable companies by market capitalization at the close on November 13, 2026, using data from CompaniesMarketCap.

Anthropic, which is not yet publicly traded, is shown at its fully diluted valuation at the top of its IPO price range. That figure multiplies $78, the top of its $70 to $78 per-share range, by about 18 billion shares. These include roughly 13 billion shares outstanding after the offering, plus stock options, restricted stock units, and shares reserved for employee stock plans, as detailed in Anthropic’s IPO filing.

Anthropic Would Join the Trillion-Dollar Club at No. 12

Apple (AAPL) is the world’s most valuable company at $5.2 trillion, about $1.2 trillion ahead of Nvidia (NVDA). The 10 largest companies alone account for 54% of the top 50’s combined $52.2 trillion value.

Anthropic would enter at No. 12, between Tesla (TSLA) and Eli Lilly (LLY), making it one of 16 companies worth at least $1 trillion. The company is expected to price its shares on November 18 and begin trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on November 19, according to CNBC.

Anthropic’s potential valuation reflects extraordinary growth expectations. According to its IPO filing, revenue reached $33.2 billion in the first nine months of 2026, more than 13 times the $2.5 billion reported a year earlier.

At $1.4 trillion, Anthropic would sit $132 billion behind Tesla and $124 billion ahead of Eli Lilly. It would be worth about 1.5 times JPMorgan Chase (JPM) ($919 billion), the world’s most valuable bank and one of the largest banks by assets held.

Only two companies based outside the U.S. would be larger than Anthropic: TSMC (TSM) ($2.1 trillion) and Saudi Aramco ($1.7 trillion).

AI Spending Is Reshaping the Most Valuable Companies

Ten of the 50 most valuable companies design or manufacture semiconductors or build the machines that produce them, including Nvidia, TSMC, Broadcom (AVGO), Samsung (SSNLF), and ASML. Together, they are worth $12.4 trillion, about 24% of the top 50’s combined value.

The scale of AI spending helps explain those valuations. Anthropic alone has committed about $901 billion in purchases and leases, which its filing says are “substantially all” related to computing and infrastructure.

Anthropic is the second AI-linked newcomer to the ranking this year. SpaceX, which absorbed Elon Musk’s AI company xAI in February, listed on Nasdaq in June and now ranks seventh at $1.9 trillion. Anthropic’s arrival would push chip equipment maker Applied Materials (AMAT) ($294 billion) out of the top 50.

Both AI newcomers are American, reinforcing U.S. dominance of the ranking. American companies account for $42.7 trillion in market value, including established businesses such as Walmart (WMT) in Arkansas and Eli Lilly in Indiana, which are also the most valuable companies in their home states.

China ranks a distant second, with six companies worth $2.4 trillion combined. Four are state-owned banks, and their combined market capitalization is less than half of Apple’s alone.

data.title: Gold Falls To 14‑month Low Below $3,750 On Hawkish Fed Rhetoric
data.description:
Gold price (XAU/USD) remains under selling pressure near $3,735 during the early Asian session on Thursday. The precious metal falls to its lowest level since September 2025 as hawkish Federal Reserve (Fed) signals raised expectations of higher interest rates.

According to Fed meeting minutes released Wednesday, officials said in October that additional interest rate increases would be needed to combat inflation, but decided to hold off while gathering more data.

The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) held the Federal Funds Rate steady at 3.75%–4.00% at its October policy meeting in a 10–2 vote. This followed a 25 basis points (bps) rate hike in September.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller reiterated his belief that the FOMC should consider a half-point hike in December. Meanwhile, Fed officials John Williams and Alberto Musalem also signaled further rate hikes may be needed to curb inflation.

"Gold won't find much relief from the Fed minutes as the overwhelming majority sees further hikes, with a couple broaching a 50bps move if inflation disappoints. Fed will hike until inflation turns, but it's not an emergency. Barring a quick reversal, today's damage suggests a probe of 3350-3450 in the coming weeks," independent analyst Tai Wong said.

Markets are now pricing in nearly a 90% chance of a 25-basis-point Fed rate hike in December, while there's a 10% odds of a larger 50-basis-point increase, according to the CME FedWatch tool. Higher rates are typically negative for gold, which doesn’t pay interest.

Mixed US data keep growth expectations broadly intact

According to Deutsche Bank, the latest run of US data “painted a mixed picture of economic performance.” On the positive side, the bank highlights that “retail sales grew by +0.2% in October (vs. +0.1% expected),” suggesting consumer demand remains resilient. However, this was offset by softer activity indicators, with “industrial production unexpectedly fell -0.4% (vs. +0.1% expected), whilst the NAHB’s housing market index also fell unexpectedly to 25 in November (vs. 29 expected).” Deutsche Bank underscores that this housing gauge marked “the lowest print for the housing market index since 2012, when the economy was still recovering from the aftermath of the GFC.” Even so, they note that “with all that in hand, the Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow estimate was little changed, with the Q4 estimate moving down very slightly from an annualised 3.5% to 3.4%,” indicating that near-term growth expectations remain broadly stable despite the mixed signals.

Kashkari flags inflation miss and resilient demand, keeping DOLLAR bias cautiously supported

Kashkari’s latest remarks score 7/10 on the FXS Speechtracker, only marginally above the 6.8/10 historical average, signaling a tone broadly in line with the established baseline but with a slightly firmer policy edge. By stressing that interest rates “absolutely can impact investment levels” while acknowledging that elevated inflation stems from supply shocks yet still requires the FED to keep expectations anchored, the speech leans cautiously hawkish, especially as strong demand and a resilient job market are highlighted alongside the admission that the FED is “clearly missing on [the] inflation side” of the mandate. The observation that markets expect more hikes than officials currently project, combined with AI being cited as a key growth engine, reinforces a narrative of persistent underlying strength that tends to underpin the DOLLAR on dips.

The FXS Fed Sentiment Index slipped by 0.11 points to 150.62, signaling a minor pullback in perceived hawkishness even as the gauge remains firmly above the neutral 100 mark. This configuration suggests that, despite a slight moderation in tone, the overall policy backdrop is still clearly hawkish in the FXS Fed Sentiment Index framework, consistent with the modestly elevated FXS Speechtracker score and supportive of the DOLLAR against lower-yielding peers.

Technical Analysis: Gold retains a bearish tone under the 100-day SMA

In the daily chart, XAU/USD remains under clear bearish pressure, trading below the entire Bollinger Bands envelope, as even the lower band comes in higher. The 20-period simple moving average from the Bollinger setup and the 100-day moving average both sit well above spot, reinforcing a dominant topside cap. The Relative Strength Index (14) hovers around 31, flirting with oversold territory and hinting that while downside momentum is still in play, fresh selling could slow as conditions become increasingly stretched.

On the topside, initial resistance is located at the Bollinger lower band near $3,770, with the Bollinger mid-line around $3,975 acting as the next notable hurdle on any corrective rebound. Further up, the Bollinger upper band at about $4,180 and the 100-day moving average near $4,190 form a broader resistance area that would need to be reclaimed to ease the current bearish outlook. With no clear support levels defined by the studied indicators below the market, the metal remains vulnerable to additional downside until price can at least recover back inside the Bollinger envelope.

data.title: S&P 500 Hangs Off Cliff
data.description:
The S&P 500 is dangling off a cliff right now. Futures have traded between 7,400 and 7,800 for six and a half months.

That range is starting to crack. A breakthrough 7,300 could force professional traders to sell into the selling.

The range kicked off on May 4th. I call it a volatility box, where price pings back and forth over time.

Six and a half months in the same box builds open interest like a snowball. The SPX now carries tens of thousands of open contracts.

If the index slips outside that box, dealers have to hedge by selling into weakness. That hedging can drive a steep decline in a very short time.

We’re already through 7,400. I see sell side activity accelerating once we clear 7,300.

The risk reward is lopsided. A bounce could carry futures back to about 7,560 by the end of this week.

The downside holds several hundred points.

The options market already shows the strain. Here’s what I break down in tonight’s video:

  • The SPX priced a $154 expected move this week. We’re already about 100 points outside it with two sessions left.

  • Thursday and Friday alone still price $122 of movement into Friday’s expiration. Tomorrow’s session holds $82 of that risk by itself.

  • December and January VIX futures still aren’t in backwardation. When the fear shows up, December could jump to 23 and trade above January.

  • The VVIX sits at 118. That reading signals imminent risk.

  • Healthcare in XLV is up 20% year to date, with most of the gains in the last couple of weeks. It took a broad hit over the last two to three sessions.

  • Financials in XLF pulled in a huge flow of capital out of semiconductors. Now sellers are hitting financials too.

Correlation is starting to creep back into this market. Google (GOOGL) and Amazon (AMZN) still catch rallies, while the safe havens stop feeling safe.

The VIX sits around 24 to 25. I don’t care about that number right now.

Tomorrow’s $82 expected move tells me far more. The market is trading what’s right in front of it.

Anthropic (ANT) prices its IPO tonight and trades tomorrow at a ridiculous valuation. Don’t let that headline pull your eye off the S&P 500.

data.title: Daily Market Outlook - Thursday, Nov. 19
data.description:
Global equity markets attempted a tentative stabilization on Thursday morning as blockbuster pricing for Anthropic’s historic initial public offering provided tactical relief following five consecutive losing sessions on Wall Street. After the S&P 500 slipped 0.2% to 7,324 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 1.1% on Wednesday, US equity futures rebounded into the European open—led by a ~1.5% bounce in Nasdaq 100 contracts and ~0.8% gains in S&P 500 e-minis. Anthropic priced its Nasdaq debut (ticker: ANT) at $83 per share—well above its $70–$78 marketed range—to raise roughly $81bn in the largest IPO on record, proving that institutional capital remains hungry for frontier artificial intelligence models even as hardware sentiment wobbles.

However, regional divergence across Asia-Pacific underscored that IPO relief has not resolved underlying semiconductor stress. Taiwan’s Taiex plunged over 4.0%, forcing financial regulators to enact emergency short-selling restrictions as investors continued to mark down hardware exposure amid Nvidia’s ongoing leadership vacuum and US export-control scrutiny. Hong Kong slid ~2.0% and South Korea’s Kospi traded softly, leaving Japan’s Nikkei 225 (+0.6%) as a rare regional outperformer. European futures pointed to a modestly firmer cash open (DAX contracts near 25,870), though fragile market structure constrained conviction. With S&P 500 spot pinned below key gamma-flip thresholds (7,500–7,520) and net dealer gamma deeply negative, index price action remains mechanical and fragile: failure to sustain a reclaim of the 7,400 call wall leaves the tape vulnerable to renewed downside liquidation.

An unyielding Federal Reserve continues to govern fixed income and currency markets. Wednesday’s October FOMC minutes confirmed that nearly all officials anticipate further rate hikes to return inflation to target, with two participants even floating the risk of a 50 bps move in December if price pressures persist. Crucially, policymakers took comfort from tighter market-implied rate paths doing the Fed's heavy lifting—meaning any sustained AI-driven easing in financial conditions risks provoking a sharper monetary pushback. data.title: Disney Confirms More Layoffs After Revealing $392 Million In Severance Costs
data.description:
The Walt Disney Company's (DIS) cost-cutting efforts are far from over, even after multiple rounds of layoffs and a year of strong financial performance.

The entertainment giant has spent much of 2026 reorganizing its businesses, eliminating jobs and streamlining operations under new CEO Josh D’Amaro.

Now, fresh financial disclosures reveal just how expensive those changes have been.

Disney recorded $392 million in severance charges alone during fiscal 2026, including $212 million in its fourth quarter, according to its latest annual report.

And more job cuts are coming.

“We do expect more layoffs,” Disney Chief Financial Officer Hugh Johnston told CNBC following the company’s earnings announcement on Nov. 17.

The confirmation comes as Disney outlines an ambitious plan to generate approximately $3 billion in annual operating expense savings by fiscal 2029, even as it increases investments in its streaming, theme park, and cruise businesses.

Disney reveals $392 million severance bill as layoffs continue

Disney’s latest SEC filing shows that restructuring and impairment charges together reached approximately $1.46 billion in fiscal 2026, up from $819 million a year earlier.

Not all of those expenses were directly related to workforce reductions. The total included $1.01 billion in investment impairments, primarily associated with A+E Global Media, and $52 million in other restructuring costs.

But the severance bill alone was substantial.

The company disclosed:

  • Entertainment: $256 million in severance charges

  • Experiences: $29 million in severance charges

  • Sports: $87 million in restructuring expenses associated with severance and exiting a facility

The Sports figure includes facility-related expenses and does not represent severance alone.

The latest disclosures follow months of workforce reductions across Disney’s businesses.

As I previously reported, the company eliminated more than 1,500 positions across three rounds of layoffs between April and September. Additional cuts followed in October within Disney Experiences, including positions at Walt Disney Imagineering in California.

Earlier this month, Bloomberg reported that Disney managers had been asked to identify potential cost savings of up to 20% in certain departments, putting thousands more jobs at risk.

Disney has not disclosed how many additional employees will lose their jobs or when the next reductions will take place.

During the Nov. 17 earnings call, D’Amaro acknowledged the human impact of the restructuring.

“Changes like these are not easy, and they affect people who care deeply about Disney and have contributed so much to this company,” he said.

D’Amaro argued that these difficult decisions are necessary for Disney to operate faster and continue investing in the businesses driving its growth.

Disney outlines where $3 billion in savings will come from

Disney’s new efficiency program extends well beyond workforce reductions.

During the earnings call, Johnston identified procurement, sourcing, information technology, real estate consolidation, and shared services as areas where the company expects to reduce operating expenses.

Disney is also targeting selling, general, and administrative costs across its operating divisions and corporate functions.

“We are laser-focused on productivity and efficiency,” Johnston told analysts.

“We are all about delivering the short term and investing in the long term, not an either/or,” he said.

Most of the approximately $3 billion in annual savings will be reinvested in the company, primarily to support streaming and other direct-to-consumer services through content, technology, and marketing. A portion will also contribute directly to profitability.

Disney is also increasingly using artificial intelligence to improve efficiency.

During the call, D’Amaro said technology developed by Disney Research Studios and Industrial Light & Magic can reduce computing requirements for rendering films by approximately 30%.

“AI helps us work faster across the company,” he said.

The company is also using AI to improve design planning and operations at its theme parks.

However, Disney has not directly connected these AI initiatives to specific layoffs.

The strategy reflects what management calls its “One Disney” approach, which seeks to bring previously separate operations closer together.

Disney has already consolidated marketing and brand leadership, appointed its first chief technology officer and shifted consumer products closer to its entertainment business.

In a Nov. 17 research report shared with TheStreet, titled “Striking the right balance of growth and investment,” UBS analysts said the efficiency program should give Disney greater capacity to reinvest in streaming and Experiences while supporting profit growth.

UBS maintained its Buy rating and $133 price target, noting that Disney remains positioned for double-digit underlying earnings growth in fiscal 2027.

The bank also highlighted the company’s ability to balance investment in theme parks, cruises, and streaming with profitability improvements.

That balance is becoming increasingly important as Disney pursues aggressive expansion while continuing to reduce operating costs.

Disney+ and Hulu are coming together in December

Disney is also approaching another significant milestone in its efforts to combine businesses and streamline operations.

During the Nov. 17 earnings call, D’Amaro confirmed that Disney+ and Hulu will move to a fully unified experience beginning in December 2026.

“Disney+ and Hulu, they are coming together in one app,” D’Amaro said.

He clarified that Disney is not launching an entirely new app. Instead, the company is building on the existing Disney+ platform, with additional features expected to arrive beginning in spring 2027.

The December integration will also introduce more live sports, podcasts, and other programming, although access to certain content and add-ons will depend on subscribers’ plans.

The company has not announced that Hulu’s separate app will shut down in December.

As TheStreet reported, the integration is part of a broader strategy to make Disney+ a central destination for entertainment and increase engagement among subscribers.

The changes come as Disney continues restructuring its traditional television businesses around streaming.

The company has also been considering organizational changes affecting ABC Entertainment, Hulu Originals, 20th Television, and Freeform, as TheStreet previously reported.

Disney has not said whether the December integration will lead to further workforce reductions. But with its $3 billion annual savings target extending through fiscal 2029 and management now confirming additional layoffs, the company’s restructuring efforts are clearly not finished.

What remains uncertain for employees is which divisions will face the next reductions and how extensive those cuts will be.

data.title: Pending Home Sales Plunge To A Three Decade Low. NAR Is Puzzled, I’m Not
data.description:
NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun does not understand the obvious.

Understanding Pending Home Sales

New home sales are reported at contract signing. Existing home sales are recorded at closing.

Pending home sales represent signed contracts of existing homes that have not yet closed.

Thus, pending home sales provide insight to the grim reports that will follow.

Pending Home Sales Plunge to Three-Decade Low

The NAR reports Pending Home Sales Decreased 4.7% in October

Pending home sales in October decreased by 4.7% month-over-month and 16.7% year-over-year, according to the National Association of REALTORS® Pending Home Sales report. The report helps the real estate ecosystem—including agents, homebuyers and sellers—better understand the housing market by providing data on the level of home sales under contract.

Month-over-month pending home sales declined in all four major U.S. regions. Year-over-year pending home sales also declined in all four regions.

“October could mark the low point in contract signings for this housing cycle, as mortgage rates appear to have topped out,” said NAR Chief Economist Dr. Lawrence Yun.

“Two consecutive months of record-low pending contracts point to very sluggish fourth-quarter home sales closings, and annual existing-home sales could be the lowest since the mid-1990s,” Yun added.

“It is somewhat puzzling that home sales would fall to levels last seen three decades ago, even as the U.S. population has grown by roughly 75 million. Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans.”

Pending Home Sales Index

Bloomberg notes 63 is the lowest reading since records began in 2001.

Yun notes annual existing-home sales could be the lowest since the mid-1990s.

Hoot of the Day, Lawrence Yun Is Puzzled

I’ll take comedy for $1,000 Alex.

Home prices are up, property taxes are up, insurance is up, mortgage rates are up, inflation is up, and job growth is sluggish.

As an added bonus, neither property taxes nor homeowners is factored into the CPI or the PCE.

By any rational measure homes are the least affordable in history. Meanwhile, Zoomers and millennials are very worried about AI taking their job.

Yet, Yun is puzzled why nobody is buying homes.

What a hoot.

Existing-Home Sales Plunge to a New 16-Year

On November 12, 2026, I commented Existing-Home Sales Plunge to a New 16-Year

Existing-Home Sales are the lowest since August 2010.

NAR Chief Cheerleader

This is not a mortgage rate issue. This is a price, quality, what you get for your money, interest rate, property tax, insurance, and overall inflation issue.

The NAR should change his title from chief economist to chief cheerleader.

Key Conclusions

  1. Home prices are too high, mortgage rates are too high, or both, for most people.

  2. For years, there was a pool of price-insensitive and mortgage rate insensitive buyers, around 4 million annualized, who were able and willing to buy regardless of point one.

Last month I commented “If we see a sustained decline in the stock market, a recession, or other economic shock, point two will not hold.”

Today I note the pool price-insensitive (and mortgage rate insensitive buyers) just gave out.

The results showed that its revenue growth gained momentum. Its revenue soared by 46% YoY to $30.2 billion, with its AI-related figure rising by 79. 

A look at its segments shows the business is thriving. The Intelligent Devices Group generated more than $17.4 billion in revenue, up 17% year on year, with an operating margin of 7.1%. This growth came as the company prioritized higher-priced devices, even as the number of units sold fell. 

Indeed, its premium PCs contributed to 63% of all PC shippings during the quarter. Recent data by Gartner (IT) showed that its PC sales dropped by 22.4% to 14.9 million during the quarter. Its PC margins have also dropped because of the ongoing memory shortage.

The Infrastructure Solutions Group’s revenue surged 178%, and its AI server pipeline reached $54 billion. 

Lenovo’s AI business is being driven by American hyperscalers, neoclouds, and Asian data center companies. Some of the revenue is coming from Asian data centers, especially in places like China and Malaysia. Lenovo’s Solutions and Services Group (SSG) grew by 205 to $3.1 billion. 

Still, the company made a $713 million loss during the quarter after losing over $1.19 billion in the same period last year. The loss was driven by fair value loss of $3.9 billion on derivative financial liabilities. 

Concerns about AI growth remains

Lenovo Group and other competitors have dropped in the past few months. For example, Dell stock has plunged by 46% from its highest point this year. It has dropped to its lowest level since May 28 this year.

HP Enterprise has also dropped to $45.78, down by 37% from the year-to-date high, while Super Micro Computer (SMCI) dropped by 52% in this period. Other companies in the AI space like Micron (MU), SanDisk, and Western Digital (WDC) have all plunged.

Investors are concerned about the potential slowdown in the coming months that would impact demand for its products. 

On the positive side, there are signs that demand is continuing to grow. For example, Nvidia (NVDA)’s earnings report showed that its revenue jumped to $115 billion in the third quarter, much higher than the expected $108 billion.

The EUR/USD is correlating to the broad market which remains nervous. U.S Treasury yields remain inflated. All of these ingredients into the EUR/USD is creating a segment of Forex speculators who are anxious and likely waiting for further impetus. Volatility in the near-term is a basic assumption that is widespread.

The EUR/USD hit lows around the 1.09525 mark briefly yesterday, as of this writing the currency pair is near 1.09720 with fast price action prevalent. Speculators hoping to take advantage of the velocity in the currency pair need to be watching technical charts, but they also need to understand nervous sentiment is high. Unfortunately for retail traders if nervous emotions grow this will mean Forex could be a focal point and cause more mayhem. While it is logical to believe a reversal will occur in the EUR/USD that is noteworthy, the problem for all traders – big and small – is betting correctly on timeframes. Those looking for upside need to be careful with their wagers.

At $80 a share, Anthropic’s planned sale of 825 million shares would generate $66 billion before fees, including proceeds going to existing shareholders.

That would rise to $75.9 billion if underwriters bought all the extra shares available to them.

SpaceX’s (SPCX) June debut brought in $75 billion initially and about $85.7 billion after its underwriters exercised their option.

On that like-for-like comparison, Anthropic would need a price above $90 per share with its extra allotment fully used, or a larger offering.

The separate $26 billion private placement with investors including Google (GOOGL) and Nvidia (NVDA) boosts the total raised alongside the listing.

But the IPO record counts money raised only through the public offering itself.

Ritter sees a first-day jump in Anthropic stock

Ritter said the shares were “very likely to jump” from his hypothetical $80 offer price.

But using his estimates of a $1.5 trillion valuation and $35.2 billion in trailing 12-month revenue, investors would be paying roughly 43 times annual sales.

In plain terms, that’s about $43 in company value for every dollar Anthropic generated in revenue over the previous year, before paying for the computing power and other costs needed to serve customers.

Ritter said that multiple could look conservative next to Palantir (PLTR) or SpaceX, but “a lot of things have to go right.”

One is keeping customers willing to pay premium prices as competing AI models improve.

Investors who bought SpaceX shares at the time of the IPO haven't done well, with the stock falling 10% since its debut.

What investors are buying beyond the growth story

Ritter also pointed to Anthropic’s public benefit structure as a sign that it takes AI safety seriously.

Its directors must weigh shareholders’ financial interests alongside the interests of people affected by the company and its stated public mission.

In practice, the board has room to back a safety decision even if it slows a product launch or raises costs.

Anthropic’s prospectus says its public benefit initiatives could reduce profitability per share.

The final offer price will settle how close Anthropic gets to SpaceX’s record. For anyone buying after trading starts, a first-day jump raises the bar.

The higher the entry price, the more profit Anthropic must eventually deliver to justify it.

data.title: Physical Gold: The Ultimate Form Of Asset Ownership
data.description:
Whatever asset we hold, whether financial or real, the question of ownership security always arises. In the event of a crisis, an attack, fraud or an unforeseen event, do I still retain full ownership of my assets and the freedom to dispose of them as I see fit? When we delve deeper into this question, we enter murky territory.

Recent events have revealed new threats. Bitcoin (BTC.X) holders believed they could protect themselves by storing their assets on hardware wallets (Ledger, Trezor or others), thereby shielding themselves from the potential collapse of the platform on which they had purchased them (recall the collapse of FTX in 2022). Unfortunately, data breaches have made them targets of criminal networks, and many have fallen victim to violent home invasions. Another form of theft has recently emerged: on October 9, it was revealed that several Ledger hardware wallets sold in Asia had been compromised. Malicious components had been implanted in the devices, allowing funds to be siphoned off. The local authorised reseller (CryptoBilis), which had recently been acquired, is suspected of involvement, but is this an isolated case? Last summer, another hardware wallet manufacturer, Coldcard, was generating recovery phrases (used in the event of a lost device) through a process that was insufficiently random, allowing AI to reconstruct these phrases using limited information about the device. Tens of millions of dollars were stolen.

Should we therefore turn back to the major cryptocurrency exchanges? Not really. On October 29, Binance, the largest of these platforms, fell victim to the biggest hack in history, with $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrencies stolen. Customers suffered no losses, but the threat remains.

Should we ultimately turn to traditional banks? Doing so would mean forgetting the warning of the 2008 subprime mortgage crisis, during which the collapse of Lehman Brothers nearly triggered a chain reaction of bank failures. Other institutions have since failed, including Silicon Valley Bank in March 2023, which was, after all, the 16th-largest bank in the United States. Why did it fail? Faced with withdrawal requests from its customers, the bank was forced to sell its holdings of US Treasury securities. However, these securities had been acquired during a period of low interest rates. As rates rose, their market value fell, leaving the institution unable to meet its obligations.

This situation can now be found, to varying degrees, across Western banks: their balance sheets are filled with sovereign bonds acquired several years ago, when interest rates were low. A forced sale in an environment where interest rates stand at 5% or higher could result in substantial losses! With public debt soaring around the world, a crisis in the sovereign debt market would quickly spread to the banking sector. Holders of life insurance policies, whose funds are largely invested in sovereign debt securities, would also be directly affected.

Like cryptocurrency exchanges, banks are exposed to the risk of cyberattacks. On November 5, a French bank, Crédit Mutuel, reportedly suffered a theft of around €100 million following a sophisticated cyberattack. Customers were not affected, but such incidents could become increasingly common in the future…

When it comes to equities, ownership rights appear to be more secure, but they generally depend on banks or platforms that may themselves fail. Except in certain arrangements, investors do not hold their securities directly, but through what is known as a “trusted third party”, with all the risks that entails.

Surely real estate remains an option? Certainly, but is it a financial asset in the strict sense of the term? In the case of one's primary residence, the answer is no: you cannot sell just a portion of it, only sell it in its entirety or mortgage it. Owning several properties comes closer to holding an investment asset, but the time required to sell them is considerably longer than for the assets discussed above. Nevertheless, real estate ownership does offer a solid degree of security.

Physical gold stored outside the banking system, with full ownership and held in one's own name, offers one of the safest forms of asset ownership. Storing gold at home exposes owners to significant risks and is therefore best avoided. It is also essential to verify the provenance and authenticity of gold bars to eliminate the risk of counterfeiting using tungsten, whose density is close to that of gold. As for paper gold, it rests on a promise and is therefore best avoided. Ultimately, the non-digital nature of the yellow metal proves to be an advantage! Its unique characteristics make gold an indispensable asset.

data.title: The Final Dollar Spike Before The Crack-Up Boom
data.description:
IT IS DIFFERENT THIS TIME. IT’S A FIRST AS WELL.

To date, we have 4000+ years of recorded commerce with banking and interest rates, 300+ years of experimentation with some form of central banking/reserve currencies, and more than 50 years of an unhinged fiat monetary system. But this is the first time in human history that we are going to experience the follow-on effects of the loosening part of a credit cycle (under a worldwide fiat currency system) that started bottoming earlier this decade, when the 30-year Treasury rate hit a nadir of 0.7% in 2020.

Even after the start in 1971 of the fiat system, the first decade and a half was really dealing with the effects of credit loosening that happened during the Gold Exchange Standard of the 1960s, with the advent of Guns AND Butter, i.e., the Vietnam War, as well as the Great Society program that included the War on Poverty, Medicare, and Medicaid. It was not until the Maestro, Alan Greenspan, came along that the world embarked on a unidirectional experiment with easy money (as evidenced by falling 30-year Treasury rates and rising national debt).

With no real-world examples of what lies ahead, how then do we extrapolate it? Fortunately, we are in the good hands of Von Mises and Rothbard’s “Austrian Business Cycle Theory”, or, as it is more commonly referred to, the “Boom-Bust Cycles of Monetary Inflation”.  Besides, there is extensive evidence that the first two smaller boom-bust cycles, as explained below and leading up to today’s crescendo, have indeed panned out as forecasted in ABCT.

1990 to 2022 – THE GREAT MONETARY EASING CYCLE WITHOUT A PAYBACK

A short summary of how the Business Cycle works is given below

  1. The lowering of interest rates by the US Fed results in malinvestments (leading to supply in excess of demand, as would be mandated by genuine savings) being made. These investments would eventually have to be liquidated, resulting in the bust.

    • Good examples of the malinvestments would be the internet infrastructure created around the year 2000 as part of Nasdaq’s Irrational Exuberance Another good example of excess supply is the 2008 housing bubble.

  2. The malinvestments are the result of an excess supply of money and credit directed towards specific industries/assets. This credit eventually spills over into consumer prices, forcing the Federal Reserve to hike rates. This intermediary, temporary tightening (within the overall easing of the 30-year easing cycle from 1990) brings about the bust and eventually leads to a recession.

  3. If the recession is allowed to run its course without any fiscal and monetary interventions, then the malinvestments of the prior period are cleared by the markets and the economy restarts on a more balanced foundation. But invariably, governments intervene, prolonging and worsening the structural imbalances.

  4. The cycle of boom-bust keeps repeating till we reach the point that Mises referred to as the “Crack Up Boom,” i.e., hyperinflation. Any easing attempted at this point would result in a rapid decline in the currency’s purchasing power.

  5. Some facets of the boom-bust cycle are given below for a better understanding.

    • The later cycles of monetary easing need increasingly greater stimulus to produce the desired effects. For example, an interest rate of 3% for a couple of years led to the NASDAQ 2000 bubble. The easing after the dotcom bust required a 1% interest rate to stimulate the economy. The easing required after the GFC in 2008 was, of course, on a logarithmic scale higher than the previous round. With nearly 15 years of ZIRP coupled with Quantitative easing, and a near 10-fold increase in the US Fed Balance sheet, the monetary stimulus required to bring about a semblance of stability was unprecedented.

    • The extent of the bust or the depth of the recession is proportional to the monetary stimulus that led to the artificial boom. It stands to reason that the malinvestments that need to be liquidated are indeed a function of the stimulus applied. The recession of 2000, after the dotcom crash, was indeed bigger than those of the 1980s and 1990s, but pales in comparison to the Great Financial Crisis of 2008.

Which brings us to the here and now. What type of recession/depression are we looking at ahead when the current malinvestments have to be liquidated? We will get to that in a while, after comparing the prior bubbles with the current ones.

 

A COMPARISON OF BUBBLES

A few short comments on the above comparison would be helpful before we proceed further.

  1. The size of current bubbles is much larger as compared to the previous cycle bubbles. This follows from the fact that the size of the economic stimulus has been much greater, leading to greater levels of malinvestments.

  2. Perhaps more than the size/scale of bubbles, it is the changing credit conditions that will cause much greater disruptions to the markets on account of the bubbles bursting.

  3. The current bubbles are winding down under conditions of tightening credit, increasing price inflation, increasing 30-year Treasury rates, and an economy on the verge of a depression rather than a severe recession.

  4. The traditional fiscal/monetary policy tools (rate cuts, QEs, etc.) used to handle the previous cycle’s bubbles bursting would be ineffective. Indeed, would probably be very counterproductive, leading to a swift destruction of the purchasing power of the US Dollar.

  5. An economic depression, with cumulative GDP contraction in excess of 25%, is the best-case scenario for the US. In all probability, this would be accompanied by very high price inflation, but is not outright Hyperinflation.


HOW DID THE US EVEN END UP HERE? WHAT WENT WRONG AND WHERE?

We can start the blame game with Greenspan, and it would indeed be very appropriate to do so. Given his understanding of Austrian economics, as he wrote so eloquently in “Gold and Economic Freedom”, Greenspan would have known that the state today would be the endgame. The Road of Monetary Easing provides no easy U-turns.

But why step on his grave when we have equally culpable individuals around us? If Gold and Economic Freedom were an intellectual masterpiece, the Courage to Act is its Antithesis. Bernanke often quotes, and supposedly draws inspiration from, Walter Bagehot’s “Lombard Street: A Description of the Money Market”.

Most Austrian economists despise the idea of a central bank and believe its functions fundamentally violate individual property rights. But given the reality of existence, I suspect most would agree with Bagehot’s proposal for a central bank’s role in a crisis: “lend freely against good collateral at a high rate of interest.”

Whatever happens in the months ahead is a direct outcome of Greenspan’s initial monetary easing actions, carried on in increasing spades by every successive Fed Bank Chair without exception. This is the result of more than 30 years of loose monetary policy, artificially low interest rates, and an unhinged US Federal Government Spending plan through the decades.

Courage for a Central Banker is to keep real interest rates high in the face of political opposition. When price inflation in the US was around 13% during 1980-81, Volcker hiked the Fed funds rates to more than 20%, offering a real yield of nearly 8%. What Bernanke did at the helm was keep real interest rates negative throughout his tenure. This is not courage. A more appropriate title for his book Courage to Act would be A Sellout to the Banking Cartel.

 

THE US DOLLAR’s ENDGAME

While it’s important to understand why the CRB Bubble has been replaced by a bubble in US Bonds today, the explanation would have to be extensive and perhaps beyond the interests of most readers. An easier way would be to just look at data – the relative valuation of Commodities vis-à-vis financial assets.

On a relative basis, Commodities today, and despite the CRB index nearly quadrupling over the last 6 years, remains at levels below those of 1970 and 2000 – the two previous bear market bottoms in the space of commodities.

I don’t have a crystal ball for when precisely the HB2.0 and AI bubbles will burst. Or as to what event would trigger the same. At least on valuations, we are well below the peak in median housing prices. The SpaceX post-IPO sugar rush might well have been the peak of the AI bubble.

In the recent sell-offs, the dollar has strengthened against other currencies and gold. This is a typical market reaction when market players deleverage existing speculative positions (AI trades, housing-related investment positions) and their safe trades (gold and commodities). Few realize that swapping gold for dollars at this point is perhaps the worst strategic swap one can make given the setup. Gold is well on its way as the rightful choice as the Numero Uno Neutral Reserve Asset, while the US Dollar is on the verge of a Crack Up Boom and possibly becoming confetti. 

What is certain is that when the bubbles burst, the Fed would have no option but to double down on QEs. Especially with the market constraint on how low interest rates can be pushed, given prevailing price inflation. In the reflation trade, even with very conservative projections, the bull market ahead in commodities is going to be one for the record books.

data.title: FX Daily: Higher US Real Rates Dominate
data.description:
US short-dated real interest rates are pushing back to their highest levels since 2023 as markets get the message that the Fed is ready to apply the brakes. These high real rates are sucking funds out of asset classes like precious metals and are triggering a broader fallout across emerging market currencies. There is no reason to fight this trend near term.

Higher US real rates are sucking funds into the dollar.

USD: Two-year real swap rates are now 2.4%

The market has got the message. We understand the Fed needs to take rates higher to get inflation back to target. And we are now seeing US two-year real rates (swap rates less the zero-coupon inflation swap) pushing above 2.40%. The last time rates were at this level was in 2023. Higher real rates are especially negative for zero-yielding precious metals and one of the reasons why gold and silver and linked currencies like the South African rand and Thai baht are under pressure.

On the Fed, we have seen further comments from Chris Waller alongside the release of the October FOMC minutes over the last 24 hours. Waller has now turned ultra-hawkish and is pushing for more than a reversal of the 75bp 'insurance' rate cuts seen last year. However, he may be out on his own here. According to the FOMC minutes, only a 'couple' of Fed voters favoured a faster pace of tightening at the October meeting and the market now looks quite settled on pricing 25bp hikes in December, January and next summer. When could these views be challenged? Perhaps not until energy-softened November CPI data is released on 10 December.

This all seems a very positive story for the dollar then. There has also been speculation that foreign interest in Anthropic's blockbuster IPO has seen some demand for the dollar this week. If that is the case, that dollar demand could wane into tomorrow once IPO allocations are settled. Yet there are good reasons for the dollar to be at current levels, and DXY advancing to the 104.60 area remains our bias for now.

For today, all eyes will be on how Anthropic (ANT) trades on its first day, while low initial jobless claims should point to a solid US jobs market.

EUR: Macro resilience, but swamped by the dollar

EUR/USD is consolidating under 1.10 as the strong dollar dominates across the board. EUR/USD price action masks ongoing resilience on the macro side, where business confidence remains relatively high and better-than-expected eurozone growth rates this year are projected to continue into 2027. As above, it is hard to see the strong dollar trend turning before mid-December, and we think EUR/USD still risks a drop to the 1.0880 area.

A light data calendar today just sees the release of September eurozone current account data. High energy prices in September may have weighed further on the surplus, although Germany delivered a surprisingly stronger current account surplus that month.

ZAR: SARB to leave rates on hold today

The South African Reserve Bank meets to set interest rates today. Having hiked interest rates to 7.25% in September, no one is expecting a further hike today. However, money markets do price another 25bp hike in early 2027. Unlike Banxico, the SARB has been responsive to the inflation shock and we see much greater scope for the rand to bounce back than Mexico's peso. See a more in-depth discussion on the rand's prospects in our 2027 FX Outlook.

MXN: Lack of rate protection comes home to roost

At one point, USD/MXN was nearly 3% higher on the day as large parts of the emerging market complex succumbed to the strong dollar. We heavily discussed the risk of peso underperformance in our 2027 Latam FX Outlook, given that Banxico had cut the policy rate spread protection over the Fed to very slim levels. We see no reason for USD/MXN to turn lower until the broader dollar trend turns. And, ultimately, that may not be until the second quarter of next year, when US inflation is substantially falling.

The S&P 500 outlook 2027 is becoming a major debate among institutional investors. While UBS and Goldman Sachs expect further gains, Panmure Liberum warns that higher interest rates, expensive valuations and slowing AI investment could trigger a substantial market correction.

The difference between an optimistic 8,900 target and a bearish 5,000 forecast highlights how uncertain the next phase of the US equity bull market could be.

UBS and Goldman Sachs Lead the Bullish S&P 500 Target 2027 Forecasts

UBS maintained its S&P 500 year-end forecast 2027 at 8,900 on November 10, implying approximately 17.7% upside from the November 13 closing price of 7,561.67.

UBS strategist Keith Parker expects earnings growth and a recovery in investor confidence to support equities. The bank forecasts S&P 500 earnings per share (EPS) of $430 in 2027, representing 18% growth, followed by $490 in 2028.

Meanwhile, the Goldman Sachs S&P 500 forecast 2027 places the index at 8,700 over the next 12 months, implying approximately 15.1% upside from the November 13 close.

Goldman expects US earnings growth to slow from 36% in 2026 to 11% in 2027. However, it believes improving valuations, economic growth and potentially lower borrowing costs could support further gains. he said,

"From here, we expect equities to ​generate positive returns, albeit with higher volatility than in ​recent years,"

Other institutional forecasts are similarly optimistic:

  • Wells Fargo Investment Institute: 8,600 to 8,800 by year-end 2027.

These targets suggest that major institutions generally expect the broader US equity market to extend its advance, although their forecast periods and assumptions differ.

Panmure Liberum Warns of a Bearish 5,000 Target

Not every investment bank expects the S&P 500 to continue climbing.

Panmure Liberum research analyst Joachim Klement forecasts the index could fall to 5,000 by the end of 2027, representing approximately 33.9% downside from its November 13 close.

His bearish outlook reflects concerns about persistent inflation, elevated bond yields and the possibility that the AI investment boom could lose momentum.

The concern is particularly relevant because technology companies have contributed significantly to recent index gains.

He warned that continued monetary tightening could bring the current equity bull market closer to its end.

The bearish forecast stands in sharp contrast to UBS's 8,900 target, illustrating the uncertainty surrounding the S&P 500 prediction 2027.

S&P 500 EPS 2027 Forecast: Earnings Growth Remains Critical

Corporate earnings will be one of the biggest drivers of the S&P 500's performance in 2027.

EPS, or earnings per share, measures how much profit a company generates for each outstanding share. For the S&P 500, aggregate earnings growth helps investors assess whether higher index valuations are supported by corporate profitability.

UBS expects index EPS to reach $430 in 2027, representing 18% annual growth.

Goldman Sachs, meanwhile, expects US earnings growth to slow to 11% in 2027 from 36% in 2026.

This difference matters because slower earnings growth could limit further valuation expansion, even if companies remain profitable.

The price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio, which measures how much investors pay for each dollar of earnings, also plays an important role.

UBS strategist Keith Parker noted that the S&P 500's forward P/E ratio declined approximately 20% during 2026, despite strong earnings growth.

UBS argues that this valuation adjustment could create room for further gains. However, Goldman warns that slowing AI capital expenditure could affect technology-related earnings and increase market volatility.

AI Investment and Treasury Yields Could Determine the Market Direction

Artificial intelligence investment and interest rates remain two major variables behind the competing S&P 500 year-end forecast 2027 scenarios.

Goldman Sachs expects AI capital expenditure growth to peak, potentially slowing earnings momentum among companies benefiting from data-centre and semiconductor spending.

UBS also identifies slowing AI investment and another increase in Treasury yields as major downside risks.

Higher bond yields can make equities less attractive because investors receive better returns from government securities. They can also reduce the present value of future corporate earnings, putting additional pressure on growth-stock valuations.

The US 10-year Treasury yield stood at 5.143% on November 16, 2026, according to Reuters-reported market data.

data.title: Risk Is Cheap, Safety Isn’t
data.description:
We tweeted the graphic below to show just how cheap NVDA shares have gotten compared to Walmart. While many replies agree with our view, quite a few didn’t.

Some of our critics argue that Nvidia’s earnings growth will not come close to the 65% annual pace analysts expect, making the stock far riskier than a steady, dependable defensive stock like Walmart. We agree, Nvidia may fall short of the lofty forecasts. However, the important analysis for investors is a deep dive into the combination of valuations and expectations.

The analysis we share is a valuation comparison of NVDA to WMT, not a comparison of either stock to the market or any other stock. It is incredibly instructive to show how valuations and expectations play into investment strategy.

A stock’s PEG ratio divides a company’s P/E by its expected five-year earnings growth. Using trailing P/E ratios, Walmart trades at 45 times earnings with expected growth of 11%, for a PEG of 4.09. Nvidia, at 17 times earnings with 65% expected growth, has a PEG of 0.26. For Nvidia’s PEG to equal Walmart’s, it only needs to grow earnings by about 4.2% per year over five years. That is only about 10% of current expectations and even half of Walmart’s.

Here’s another way to think about it. If Walmart shares stay the same price for five years and it achieves its expected 11% growth, its P/E falls to about 26.7. Nvidia’s P/E would also be 26.7 if its earnings declined by over 8% a year.

So yes, we are comfortable taking the “risk” that Nvidia doesn’t meet earnings growth expectations versus the “safety” of Walmart. Simply, the market is providing a lot of cushion for being wrong.

What To Watch Today

IPO

Anthropic (ANT) prices Wednesday evening and is scheduled to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market today. Proposed range: $70 to $78 per share, 825 million Class A shares. Settlement Friday, November 20.

Economy

Earnings

Fed Speakers

Hammack 8:50 a.m. · Goolsbee 12:30 p.m. · Barr 2:15 p.m. · Barkin 4:00 p.m. · Paulson 6:30 p.m. (all ET)

Market Trading Update

On Tuesday, we laid out the supply side of the Anthropic IPO and why roughly $90 billion of new stock matters more than the valuation debate. This morning, the deal goes live. Anthropic (ANT) priced last night and opens for trading on Nasdaq today. The question I’m getting most is simple. Should you buy it?

History gives a fairly blunt answer. Back in June, the Bull Bear Report warned readers to wait on the SpaceX IPO because big debuts usually sell off in the first couple of months. SpaceX (SPCX) priced at $135, jumped 19% on day one, and closed at $201.80 on June 16. By August 5, it had closed at $108.27, a 46% decline from the peak. On Monday, it finished at $137.36, barely above the offer price five months later.

That wasn’t bad luck. Such is the nature of new issues. The table below, rebuilt from Carson Investment Research, tracks 36 major IPOs since Google in 2004. The average first-day gain was 49%, and 92% closed higher on day one. The average maximum drawdown in the first 12 months was 55%, and NOT one of these companies escaped a decline of at least 13%.

The reasons are mechanical. Floats are tiny at the start, so modest buying moves the price a lot. Then supply arrives as lockups expire and insiders sell. Anthropic is selling 825 million shares, roughly 5% of its fully diluted share count, a float about the size of SpaceX’s. Sentiment is running hot, too. On Monday, a crypto contract tracking ANT on Hyperliquid traded at $98.67, and CNBC reported Tuesday that demand is likely to push prices above the $70-$78 range.

None of this says Anthropic is a bad company. It says the first few months of a “hot” IPO are usually the worst time to own it. If you want exposure, here are the rules we’d follow:

  1. Don’t buy the open. Let price discovery and the first-day pop play out.

  2. Use limit orders only. Market orders on debut day are an invitation to overpay.

  3. Start small. A starter position of 1% or less limits the damage if history repeats.

  4. Build in thirds. Add after the first earnings report, after analyst coverage begins, and after the first lockup expires.

  5. Calendar the lockups. Know when insider supply hits the market.

  6. Define the exit before the entry. Decide what price or event proves you wrong.

Our portfolios will sit out the debut. We’d rather pay a little more later with real information than pay a premium today for a story.

The pop is the marketing. The drawdown is the tuition.

Nvidia Kills It: Investors Aren’t Jumping For Joy

Nvidia delivered a near-perfect quarter, and the market responded with a rather tame golf clap. Revenue of $115.8 billion rose 103% from a year ago and beat the roughly $109 billion consensus. Further, management guided the coming quarter about $5 billion higher than prior expectations, and the board added $150 billion to the buyback authorization. Shares opened Wednesday morning about 3% higher but turned negative within the first hour of trading, as we share below. Not what one would expect given the excellent results.

Investors have ample reason to be reserved. For starters, gross margin guidance fell to 72% from nearly 75% this quarter. On $130 billion of revenue, three points of margin is roughly $4 billion of gross profit. Rising memory costs are the likely culprit. Further, long-term debt climbed to $32.4 billion from $7.5 billion at fiscal year-end, meaning Nvidia is now borrowing while it repurchases stock and finances its customers. Lastly, and most importantly, the company has no permanent chief executive, and an independent board committee investigation remains open with a wide range of potential outcomes, some of which can be problematic for the company.

Here is what we find most telling. CoreWeave rose about 5.4% and Nebius about 7%, both outpacing Nvidia itself. They are very beaten up, but it’s a vote of confidence that one of their key financiers (NVDA) will continue to provide financing.

Buy And Forget? It’s Not That Easy

Buy an S&P 500 index fund, set up automatic contributions, and forget about it. It’s one of the most common pieces of retirement advice, and the chart below makes a strong case for it. In January 1940, the S&P 500, as reconstructed by Robert Shiller, stood at about 12. Today, it’s around 7,500. World War II, regional wars, recessions, oil shocks, a pandemic, and a long list of financial crises look like minor speed bumps. For anyone saving for retirement, the answer seems obvious: why do anything other than buy and forget?

Unfortunately, it’s not that easy. The chart shows what the market did over 86 years. It doesn’t show what happened to investors who depended on it during the 20 or 30 years that mattered most to them.
