data.title: Q3 2026 U.S. Retail Scorecard – Update
data.description:
To date, 146 of the 183 companies in our LSEG Retail/Restaurant Index have reported their EPS results for Q3 2026, representing 78% of the index. Of those companies that have reported their quarterly results, 68% announced profits that beat analysts’ expectations, while 2% delivered on-target results and 30% reported earnings that fell below estimates. The Q3 2026 blended earnings growth estimate now stands at 8.3%.

The blended revenue growth estimate for the 146 companies in this index is 6.3% for Q3 2026. Of those companies that have reported their quarterly results so far, 59% announced revenue that exceeded analysts’ expectations and the remaining 41% reported that their revenue fell below analysts’ forecasts.

Exhibit 1: LSEG Earnings Dashboard

This week in retail

Target’s (TGT) turnaround is gaining traction, TJX continues to benefit from value-seeking consumers, and Lowe’s (LOW) is seeing stronger digital and professional customer demand despite earnings pressure.

As predicted by StarMine, Target delivered a stellar Q3 performance, providing compelling evidence that its turnaround strategy is gaining traction as its refreshed merchandise assortment resonates with consumers. The discounter exceeded earnings, revenue, and same-store sales (SSS) expectations, with earnings surging 48.9% from a year ago and revenue increasing 7.1%. SSS rose a robust 5.6%, supported by a 5.0% increase in customer traffic, suggesting that Target is successfully attracting shoppers back to its stores. Digital comparable sales also increased nearly 10%, reinforcing the retailer’s growing omnichannel momentum.

Importantly, sales increased in all three months of the quarter, with the strongest performance during the back-to-school season. Beauty remained a standout category, posting 9% sales growth, while food and beverage sales increased nearly 7%. Encouraged by the broad-based improvement, Target raised its full-year earnings guidance to $10.65–$11.40 per share, up from its previous range of $9.90–$10.90. Management also expressed optimism heading into the critical holiday shopping season.

The results suggest Target’s turnaround is beginning to translate into tangible improvements in customer traffic, merchandise demand, and profitability. The strong traffic gains are particularly encouraging, indicating that growth is being driven by more shoppers rather than simply higher spending per visit.

Meanwhile, TJX delivered another solid quarter, with earnings matching expectations and revenue increasing 5.5% from a year ago. Same-store sales rose a healthy 4.0%, comfortably exceeding the 2.8% consensus estimate. The results reinforce the continued appeal of off-price retail as consumers across income groups remain focused on finding compelling value.

Notably, trends improved at Marmaxx, the company’s largest division, which includes T.J. Maxx, Marshalls, and Sierra in the U.S. The improvement is particularly encouraging following the merchandising challenges that weighed on the division’s performance in the previous quarter. Management raised its full-year outlook and anticipates stronger sales momentum during the holiday season, underscoring confidence in its merchandise assortment and ability to capture demand from value-conscious shoppers.

On the other hand, Lowe’s reported a more mixed Q3 performance. Earnings declined 9.8% from a year ago, although revenue increased a healthy 9.3%. SSS rose 1.8%, exceeding the 0.4% consensus estimate and signaling improving demand despite continued pressure across the broader home improvement market.

E-commerce was a particularly bright spot, with online sales surging 17.4%, marking the retailer’s fifth consecutive quarter of double-digit digital growth and its third straight quarter of growth exceeding 15%. Management also highlighted solid performance in its Pro and home services businesses, as both professional contractors and DIY customers increasingly engage with Lowe’s across digital and physical channels.

The company also benefited from approximately $250 million in tariff-related benefits during the quarter. Supported by stronger comparable sales and digital momentum, Lowe’s raised its full-year guidance, suggesting growing confidence in its ability to navigate a challenging home improvement environment.

Taken together, the results reinforce a central theme of this earnings season: consumers are still spending, but retailers must deliver the right combination of value, merchandise, and convenience to capture that demand. Target’s strong traffic growth suggests its turnaround is resonating with shoppers, while TJX continues to capitalize on consumers’ appetite for discounted branded merchandise. Meanwhile, Lowe’s robust digital performance underscores the growing importance of convenience, even in traditionally store-driven categories such as home improvement. The divergence highlights that successful retail execution, not simply the strength of the consumer, is increasingly determining which companies outperform.

data.title: Anthropic IPO Prices At $83 A Share As ANT Prepares Thursday Debut
data.description:
Anthropic has priced its initial public offering at $83 a share, according to CNBC and Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter, $5 above the top of the $70–$78 range in the company's latest SEC filing.

Class A shares in the Claude developer are due to begin trading on Thursday, 19 November, on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker ANT.

The $83 price has not yet been locked in a prospectus supplement.

As of late evening in London on 18 November, no Form 424B4 had appeared on EDGAR, and Anthropic had not published a pricing announcement on its newsroom or IPO site.

Until a filing appears, these figures should be read as reported terms, not as a confirmed prospectus price.

Bloomberg also said the size of the offering has increased, without disclosing a new share count.

The marketed deal, in Amendment No. 3 to Anthropic's Form S-1, filed on 17 November, was 825 million Class A shares — 801,351,354 sold by the company and 23,648,646 by existing holders.

On that marketed count, $83 a share would raise $68.475 billion before underwriting discounts, an Invezz calculation.

Actual gross proceeds would be higher if the deal was upsized, as Bloomberg reported. Anthropic would not receive the proceeds from the secondary shares. A separate $26 billion private placement of non-voting Class N shares is due to close at the IPO price.

How does $83 compare with the filed range?

The official range was never raised in a filing. Amendment No. 3 still estimated $70.00 to $78.00 a share. At $78, the 825 million shares would have raised $64.35 billion gross, as set out in our note on Anthropic's $70–$78 IPO price range.

Earlier on Wednesday, CNBC reported that Anthropic was considering selling more than 825 million shares and was weighing a price well above $80.

The Wall Street Journal had reported on 17 November that Anthropic expected to price above $80, and said that would value the company at about $1.5 trillion to $1.6 trillion.

The prospectus granted the underwriters, represented by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, a 30-day option to buy up to 123.75 million additional Class A shares. Whether that greenshoe was resized with any upsizing of the base deal has not been disclosed.

What valuation does $83 imply?

The filing does not state a single official valuation, and the final figure will depend on the share count used, including any upsizing.

Coverage of the prospectus has put the fully diluted value at about $1.405 trillion at the $78 top of the range. A like-for-like move to $83 would imply about $1.50 trillion. That is an illustration, not a number in a pricing prospectus, and it would change if more shares have been added.

How strong was demand?

CNBC reported on Wednesday morning that institutional demand was around $400 billion and that retail demand was approaching $100 billion. Those figures were described as indications of interest, not binding orders.

What happens next?

Trading is scheduled to start on Thursday under the ANT ticker. Nasdaq, in Data Technical News #2026-28, said Anthropic's Class A common stock is expected to begin trading on 19 November.

Hargreaves Lansdown has told UK applicants that trading is expected from 2:30pm London time (9:30am ET). Investors who received an allocation pay the IPO price; anyone buying once the shares are listed pays the market price. A Form 424B4, when it appears, would be the official confirmation of the price, the final share count and any change to the greenshoe.

If ANT starts trading on 19 November, MSCI has said it would decide on early inclusion no later than before the open of the third trading day, which would be Monday, 23 November. If the stock qualifies, addition would be effective as of the close on 30 November, or 1 December.

FTSE Russell has deferred fast entry because of Thanksgiving: Russell US addition, if confirmed, would be effective 14 December, and FTSE GEIS on 21 December. Nasdaq has not issued a notice adding ANT to the Nasdaq-100. The S&P 500 is not in prospect at listing.

Thursday's first trade will test whether that demand holds up in public.
